64.title: Kumbhakarna wakes
64.hook: the giant who sleeps, and the three qualities in every heart
64.carry: tamas: seeing what's right, and sleeping through it
64.howItsDone: Kumbhakarna's waking is a favorite, often comic scene in Ramlila plays and children's retellings, and in everyday Indian speech a heavy sleeper is sometimes teasingly called a Kumbhakarna.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana falls, Hanuman flies the mountain back, and Rama holds him like a brother. Bhakti.
screen: `BHAKTI: GOD HOLDS HIS DEVOTEE LIKE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Everybody knows someone who's impossible to wake up. Ravana is losing. His generals are dead, his city is surrounded, and he has one option left. Deep in the palace, his brother is asleep: Kumbhakarna, a giant so huge that when he stands up, the story says, he's like a mountain walking. He sleeps for months at a time. So Ravana sends servants to wake him. A new week starts with the hardest alarm clock in literature.
screen: `IMPOSSIBLE TO WAKE.` → `THE GIANT ASLEEP IN THE PALACE.` → `THE HARDEST ALARM CLOCK.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, waking him is almost comic. Demons pile mountains of food and jars of drink by his nose. They beat drums, blow conches, roar. They drive elephants over his body. Finally he yawns, and wakes up hungry. Why does he sleep like that? In Valmiki's last book, Ravana, Kumbhakarna and their younger brother Vibhishana each do fierce austerities, and the creator god Brahma offers each a boon. Ravana asks that no god or demon can kill him; he doesn't bother to mention humans. Kumbhakarna is about to ask, and the gods panic, so the goddess of speech, Sarasvati, enters his mouth, and out comes a wish for sleep. Later tellings make it a slip of one syllable: indrasana, Indra's throne, came out as nidrasana, a bed of sleep. And Vibhishana asks for this: that his mind stay on dharma, on what's right, even in the worst trouble. Three brothers, three wishes. Hindu teaching names three qualities, the gunas, woven through every person: sattva, clear and bright; rajas, restless wanting; tamas, heavy and dull, the pull to sleep. Many teachers read the brothers as those three: Ravana's rajas, Vibhishana's sattva, Kumbhakarna's tamas. Awake, the giant hears what Ravana has done and tells him straight: you were wrong to take Sita. This is your own doing. And then, out of loyalty to his brother, he goes out and fights for the wrong cause anyway, until Rama's arrows bring him down and his fall shakes the earth. That's tamas. Not stupidity: heaviness, darkness, the dulling of what you already know. All three live in each of us. Tamas is the part that knows you should call your grandmother back, and rolls over anyway.
screen: `DRUMS, ELEPHANTS, MOUNTAINS OF FOOD.` · `THREE BROTHERS, THREE WISHES.` · `SATTVA, RAJAS, TAMAS.` · `HE SEES IT. HE FIGHTS FOR IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Hindu tradition prizes the hour before dawn, brahma muhurta, as the clearest time of day, the time of sattva. Sit up straight for two minutes and notice which of the three is loudest in you right now: clear, restless or heavy. Don't fight it; just name it. If you pray, ask for what Vibhishana asked for: a mind that stays on what's right, even in trouble. If you don't, picture tomorrow's alarm, and getting up the first time.
Kumbhakarna wakes. Ravana's giant brother, who tells him the truth and then fights for him anyway.
Your line: tamas, seeing what's right, and sleeping through it. Kumbhakarna saw. See you tomorrow.

65.title: Ravana rides out
65.hook: the king finally comes himself; the inner enemies that grow back
65.carry: six inner enemies, and they grow back
65.howItsDone: At Dussehra, many communities in north India burn huge effigies of the ten-headed Ravana, and some teachers use the ten heads to speak about the inner faults that keep returning; the Shiva Tandava Stotram, attributed to Ravana, is chanted by devotees of Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kumbhakarna wakes, the giant who saw his brother was wrong and fought for him anyway. Tamas.
screen: `TAMAS: SEEING WHAT'S RIGHT, SLEEPING THROUGH IT.`

segments.voice: For the whole war, Ravana has sent other people. Generals. Sons. His giant brother. One by one, they've fallen. Kumbhakarna is gone. Now even Indrajit, his great son, the master of illusion, has been killed by Lakshmana. There's nobody left to send. So the king of Lanka puts on his armor, climbs into his chariot, and rides out through the gates himself. Ten heads. Twenty arms. A bow in several hands at once. After all these weeks, the serial brings the two of them face to face: Rama on foot, Ravana in the chariot.
screen: `EVERYONE HE SENT HAS FALLEN.` → `THE GATES OPEN.` → `FACE TO FACE, AT LAST.`

segments.voice: It's easy to make Ravana a cartoon, and the Ramayana doesn't. In the tradition he's a great scholar, learned in the Vedas, and a fierce devotee of Shiva; a hymn to Shiva's dance, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, is traditionally said to be his. Tradition makes him a veena player too. He's brave, and a real king to his people. And he took another man's wife by force and wouldn't give her back when everyone he trusted begged him to. That's the tragedy: all that greatness, bent around one refusal. Even his name carries a story. In the tradition, he once tried to lift Shiva's mountain, Kailasa, and Shiva pressed it down with one toe, pinning him. Ravana roared so loudly the worlds shook, and Shiva, in the Uttara Kanda's telling, named him Ravana: the one who made the worlds cry out. Now the fight. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows back in its place. He cuts another. It grows back. Over and over. Hindu teaching has a name for what keeps growing back: the six inner enemies, the shadripu. Desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy. Some teachers read Ravana's ten heads as those enemies; lists differ. Ravana had learning, devotion and courage, and it wasn't enough, because one enemy, desire, sat on the throne. That's the teaching: knowing the scriptures doesn't save you if the enemies inside are running things. It's why, at Dussehra, when the huge ten-headed effigies burn, many families say those are what's really burning. So start small: pick one, and say its name.
screen: `SCHOLAR, DEVOTEE, MUSICIAN, KING.` · `THE ONE WHO MADE THE WORLDS CRY OUT.` · `CUT ONE HEAD. ANOTHER GROWS.` · `SHADRIPU: SIX ENEMIES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Picture ten heads without fear, and give them faces you might recognize: the six enemies first, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, then whatever else yours are. Pick the one that showed up most this week, look it in the face without fighting it, and say its name quietly, inside. When it grows back, and it will, you'll recognize it faster.
Ravana, the one who made the worlds cry out: the great, learned, ten-headed king, out of people to send, finally facing Rama himself.

66.title: The last arrow
66.hook: Agastya's hymn to the sun; Rama bows to Surya; Ravana falls
66.carry: surya: the sun greeted as divine light
66.howItsDone: Devotees chant the Aditya Hridayam, the hymn Agastya teaches Rama, at sunrise or before difficult undertakings; Ravana's defeat is celebrated at Dussehra (Vijayadashami), when effigies of Ravana are burned in many towns.

screen: `SIX INNER ENEMIES, AND THEY GROW BACK.`

segments.voice: Near the end of something long, the last week of a hard job, the last exam, it gets hard to tell whether you're winning at all. The fight between Rama and Ravana has gone on and on. The gods have sent Rama a chariot, Indra's own, driven by Indra's charioteer, Matali. Ravana's heads keep growing back. And Rama, in Valmiki's telling, is worn out, and worried. Then an old sage walks onto the battlefield: Agastya. Instead of a weapon, he gives Rama words.
screen: `THE END OF SOMETHING LONG.` → `HEADS THAT KEEP GROWING BACK.` → `A SAGE WALKS ONTO THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun. Praise the sun, the sage tells him, the one who lights every world and wakes every living thing. Recite this, and worry and grief will ease. So, in the middle of a war, Rama stops. He looks at the sun and recites the hymn, and in the story, strength comes back into him. Devotees still chant it, some at sunrise, some before a hard day: the words a tired prince heard on a battlefield. Then Matali, the charioteer, speaks up. Remember the weapon made by Brahma, he says. The time has come. Rama takes out an arrow given to him long before: the brahmastra, the weapon of the creator himself. He sets it to the bow and releases it. It strikes Ravana in the chest, in the heart, and the king of Lanka falls from his chariot. The gods rain flowers. The war is over. Later tellings add nectar hidden in Ravana's navel; in Valmiki, the weapon itself does the work. Rama, whom Hindus worship as God come to earth, still stops and bows to the sun before the end. Many Hindus still greet the morning sun, Surya, palms joined, or pouring water from cupped hands toward it, with words like Om Suryaya Namah: I bow to the sun. The light that wakes every living thing, greeted as divine. Before the phone, before the news, a moment turned toward the light. And every autumn, many Hindus celebrate Rama's victory at Dussehra, the victorious tenth day.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `MATALI: THE TIME HAS COME.` · `THE LAST ARROW. RAVANA FALLS.` · `OM SURYAYA NAMAH.`

segments.voice: If you can see daylight, turn toward it; if not, face where the sun would be. Join your palms, or cup your hands as if holding water to pour toward it, and say quietly: Om Suryaya Namah, I bow to the sun. If you don't pray, just let the light reach your face and think of one hard thing in front of you this week. Rama stopped in the middle of a war to do this.
Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun: the hymn Agastya gives a tired Rama before the last arrow.
Your line: Surya, the sun greeted as divine light. Even Rama stopped for it. Day sixty-six, and the war is done.

67.title: Mandodari's lament
67.hook: Ravana's queen weeps; Rama gives the enemy his rites
67.carry: hostility ends at death; even ravana gets his rites
67.howItsDone: Mandodari is remembered in Hindu tradition as a wise and virtuous queen and is named in a well-known Sanskrit verse listing five revered women, the panchakanya, traditionally recited in the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the last arrow. Rama bowed to the sun with the Aditya Hridayam, and Ravana fell.

segments.voice: When a notorious person dies, the internet celebrates; the jokes arrive within minutes. And somewhere, off-camera, a woman sits on a kitchen floor who has just lost her husband. The war is over. The monkeys are cheering. Ravana lies on the battlefield. Out through the gates of Lanka come the women of the palace, weeping, running to his body. At the front is his chief queen, Mandodari. And the Ramayana, a story that spent weeks building Ravana up as the enemy, stops everything to let her speak.
screen: `THE JOKES ARRIVE IN MINUTES.` → `THE WOMEN RUN FROM THE GATES.` → `THE STORY LETS HER SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Mandodari is the daughter of Maya, the great architect of the demons, and in the tradition she is wise and good. In the tradition, she begged Ravana to send Sita back. He wouldn't listen. Now she kneels by his body, and Valmiki gives her lament room. She remembers his greatness: the king who conquered the gods, who made the worlds tremble. She can't believe he's lying in the dust. She tells him, in effect: I warned you. Your desire for another man's wife is what killed you. And in the same breath, she weeps for him with her whole heart. She doesn't pretend he was innocent, or that she didn't love him. Both are true at once. Then Rama does something just as striking. Vibhishana, Ravana's brother, hesitates to perform the funeral rites: why honor a man who did such wrong? Rama tells him, in Valmiki's telling, that hostility ends at death. The fight is over. He was your brother. Give him his rites. And Ravana is cremated with the honors of a king. That's a Hindu teaching, not just a kind moment: the last rites, antyeshti, the final offering, are owed to every person, and Rama puts it plainly: hostility ends at death. Every villain was somebody's son, somebody's husband. The Ramayana doesn't let you cheer at a funeral. A traditional Sanskrit verse names five honored women, the panchakanya, and Mandodari is one of them, with Ahalya, Draupadi and Tara. Her grief is honored, not mocked. Compassion for the fallen doesn't excuse anything. It just refuses to forget that someone loved him.
screen: `MANDODARI BEGGED HIM TO LISTEN.` · `I WARNED YOU. AND I LOVED YOU.` · `HOSTILITY ENDS AT DEATH.` · `EVERY VILLAIN WAS SOMEBODY'S.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who fell, someone in the news or in your family who did real harm and paid for it, and without excusing it, picture the person who loved them, a mother, a husband, a child, and what they're feeling tonight. Hold both, what was wrong and the grief. If you pray, you can hold those mourners in your prayer.

68.title: Sita and the fire
68.hook: Sita walks into the flame and out
68.carry: agni, the witness: why vows are made at the fire
68.howItsDone: Sita's trial by fire is told and debated openly in Hindu homes, temples and scholarship; devotional tellings such as Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas present a shadow Sita, while some readers, poets and women's song traditions have questioned the scene from Sita's side.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari's lament, and Rama telling Vibhishana that hostility ends at death, even for an enemy.

This is the scene people stop at. The war is won. Sita is brought out of Lanka, after all those months in the garden refusing Ravana every day. The whole army crowds around to see her. She comes to Rama. This is the reunion the entire story has been running toward. And it goes wrong. This one doesn't get tidied up. Here it is straight, then what people in the tradition have said about it, because they've been arguing about this scene for a very long time.
screen: `THE REUNION THE STORY RAN TOWARD.` → `AND IT GOES WRONG.` → `NO TIDYING THIS ONE UP.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's telling, Rama speaks coldly, in front of everyone. He says he fought to wipe out the insult to his name, and that since she lived in another man's house, he can't simply take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes. Sita is stunned. Then she answers him, and her answer is magnificent: her heart was always his; what Ravana did to her body was done by force; how could he speak to her like a common man? She turns to Lakshmana and tells him to build a fire, and she walks into the flames. The fire god, Agni, rises out of them carrying her unharmed, and declares her pure. Rama says he never doubted her; he did it, he says, so the world would have no doubt. That's the text: agni pariksha, the trial by fire. Now, how the tradition reads it. Tulsidas, in the Ramcharitmanas, tells it differently: before the abduction, the real Sita was placed in the fire's keeping, and a shadow Sita was the one taken; the fire only gives the real one back. Some devotees take comfort in that. Others read Valmiki's scene as a king bowing to public opinion, and hold that as a flaw, or a tragedy, or a test of dharma under pressure. Women have long sung and retold this story from Sita's side, questioning Rama, like the Bengali poet Chandrabati. None of these voices is outside Hinduism. They're all inside it. This tradition doesn't ask you to stop asking. And one thing every telling keeps: the fire as witness. Agni sees what's true, and it is Agni who speaks for Sita. That's why, at a Hindu wedding, the couple walks around a sacred fire: the vows are made with Agni as witness.

69.title: The return
69.hook: lamps lit across Ayodhya; the night the whole country lights up
69.howItsDone: At Diwali, on the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, Hindus light rows of clay lamps (diyas) on doorsteps, windows and rooftops; in much of north India the festival is celebrated as Rama's return to Ayodhya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: agni pariksha, Sita's trial by fire, and Agni, the witness, who carried her out.

Fourteen years. A child born the week Rama left would be a teenager now. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana climb into the Pushpaka, the flying chariot that belonged to Ravana, and head north. As they fly, Rama points down and shows Sita everything they've been through: there's the bridge. There's where Jatayu fell. There's Kishkindha. There's the forest where we lived. And far away, in a village outside Ayodhya, a man has been waiting the whole time, sleeping on the ground, ruling with a pair of sandals on the throne. His brother Bharata.
screen: `FOURTEEN YEARS.` → `THE FLYING CHARIOT HEADS NORTH.` → `BHARATA, STILL WAITING.`

segments.voice: Rama sends Hanuman flying ahead to tell Bharata they're coming. Why send word first? Because, in the story, Bharata had made a vow: if Rama didn't come back the day the fourteen years ended, he would give up his life. And the day has come. Hanuman finds him thin, in bark clothes, hair matted, living like a hermit to match his brother in the forest. Rama is coming, Hanuman says, and Bharata's joy is so great he can hardly speak. Then the whole city pours out to meet the flying chariot, and the brothers embrace. Here's where one of the biggest festivals in the world comes in. Tradition says that when Rama came home, the people of Ayodhya lit lamps on doorsteps, on walls, along the rooftops, in every window, to welcome him and light the way home. Rows and rows of little clay lamps. In Sanskrit, a row of lamps is dipavali: dipa, a lamp, and avali, a row. Say it the way it's said all over India: Diwali. Valmiki describes Ayodhya's great celebration. The lamps, for most people, come from the way the story has been lived: every autumn, on the darkest night of the month, hundreds of millions of people light them again. Not all Hindus connect Diwali mainly with Rama; other regions tell other stories, and you'll hear some on another day. But in much of north India, this is the night. Every little clay lamp on every windowsill, every year, is that night again. You don't remember it. You repeat it. Somebody's coming home. Light the way.
screen: `HANUMAN FLIES AHEAD TO BHARATA.` · `THE BROTHERS EMBRACE.` · `DIPAVALI: A ROW OF LAMPS.` · `EVERY LAMP, EVERY YEAR, IS THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a lamp, light it; if not, turn on one small light, or just picture a clay lamp on a windowsill. Look at the flame and think of someone who's been away, a child at college, a friend who drifted, a parent far away. Picture them walking up the street at night, and your light in the window showing them where home is.
Diwali. From dipavali, a row of lamps: the night Ayodhya lit up to bring Rama home.
Your line: every lamp is this night. Ayodhya's lamps are still lit, every year. Welcome home, day sixty-nine.

70.title: The sandals come down
70.hook: the coronation; the sandals come down; what a serial leaves behind
70.carry: hanuman listens wherever rama's story is told
70.howItsDone: Images of Rama's coronation (Rama pattabhishekam), with Sita beside him and Hanuman at his feet, hang in Hindu homes; at some Ramayana readings and recitations a seat is left for Hanuman, who tradition says is present wherever the story is told.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Diwali, the row of lamps that lit Rama home, and Bharata still waiting.

The last episode of a series that ran for weeks. The credits. Then a strange quiet in the room, like someone moved out. Five weeks ago, this started with an old king who had no sons. Then four boys, a bow nobody could lift, Sita choosing. Kaikeyi's two wishes. Fourteen years. A brother who put sandals on a throne. A golden deer, a line in the dust, an old bird who tried. Shabari's berries. A bridge, a squirrel, a foot nobody could move, a giant who woke, ten heads, a fire. Lamps. Today, the last episode.
screen: `THE LAST EPISODE.` → `FROM A KING WITH NO SONS...` → `...TO A CITY FULL OF LAMPS.`

segments.voice: Remember the sandals? Fourteen years ago, Bharata refused the throne, set Rama's sandals on it, and ruled as their servant. Now, in the story, he brings them back and places them on Rama's feet himself. I've kept your kingdom, he says, in effect; here it is. A brother handing back what was never his. Then the coronation. Rama sits on the throne with Sita beside him, the brothers around them, and Hanuman at his feet. The story says Rama's reign was a time when there was no fear, no untimely death, when the rains came on time. People still say Ram Rajya, the rule of Rama, to mean a just and peaceful society, and people still argue about what that should look like. Valmiki's story doesn't stop cleanly here. There's another book after this one, with some of the hardest chapters in the whole Ramayana, and you'll meet them later on the path. But this serial ends at the coronation. So what does a serial leave behind? The Ramayana answers that itself. In the Uttara Kanda, as the allies take their leave, Hanuman asks Rama for one thing: to stay alive on earth for as long as the story of Rama is told. Tradition says he's still here, one of the deathless ones, listening. That's why families read the Ramayana aloud at home and in temples, and at some readings a seat is left empty for him: wherever Rama's name is sung, Hanuman is said to come. The ending isn't really the end.
screen: `THE SANDALS COME DOWN.` · `THE CORONATION, HANUMAN AT HIS FEET.` · `RAM RAJYA: NO FEAR.` · `WHEREVER THE STORY IS TOLD, HANUMAN LISTENS.`

segments.voice: Rama's name itself is a prayer. Many Hindus repeat it softly, Sita Ram, Sita Ram, or simply Ram, a practice called japa: repeating a holy name. For two minutes, if you pray, say it quietly with your breath, and picture Hanuman sitting nearby, listening. If you don't pray, let one character from these five weeks sit with you instead, Jatayu, Shabari, the squirrel, Bharata with the sandals, and notice what stayed.
After. The sandals come down, the king is crowned, and Hanuman stays as long as the story is told.
